items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: Al Rose was telling me that when he grew up listening in the bands

ctx.x: Yeah, the Ori band always used it. Of course, Bud Scott, in the days I heard him, he always played guitar, too. He could play banjo, might have done it on a few special numbers sometime, but almost always just guitar. And the Ori band also softened down a lot at times. I mean, they had a lot of variety and dynamics, you might say. But that was part of the old New Orleans tradition, and Jelly talks about it, but Jelly also talks about they would be probably New Orleans bands, too. He was objecting to, being loud.…

Al Rose was telling me that when he grew up listening in the bands that the clarinet and the trumpet always were in harmony together, and the clarinet was not a counterpoint to the trumpet, but he rarely hears that now, that Harry Shields was the last one he knew of that actually harmonized with the trumpet player.

Yeah, occasionally some of the other musicians do it today, but to me, I never heard music here before, say 1930, 38 maybe, it was the first time I ever heard any music here. And so all we have to do, go by, are the old records. But to me, that's been more, to me, a more later development. Some people try to make a big difference between the terms like Dixieland and traditional New Orleans jazz and all, which is mainly just words in people's minds. Because like Bunk once said, we always called it ragtime, and…

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: And I was interviewing Bill Russell last night

ctx.x: To hear the Brunies band, Abbey Brunies band. I enjoyed that night very much and I was very much impressed by the music.

Well it's funny when you go back and listen to things, you reevaluate them. Oh yeah. And I was interviewing Bill Russell last night and he was talking about the masters that he rejected years ago, so I'm great now.
Oh sure. Well, of course your criteria change and the availability of the quality changes substantially, and of course we just don't have any more like we used to have to work with.

items.title: Betty Lee Hanson, Joe James, George Lewis, Joe Lewis, Joe Butler, Kid Thomas Valentine, Bill Russell, Allan…
items.q: And this is one of our friends, Al Rose, is trying to get a certain definition adopted

ctx.x: Well, what about this pure jazz that all of you are trying to preserve?

Well, there may be a little difference, a little difference in the feeling of the white and the colored. It's hard to put your finger on it, though, and say definitely, because some of the white musicians undoubtedly played the same style as the colored in the old days. Maybe the colored held on to that old time feeling a little bit better, a little bit longer than the white musicians. But today, they all call it, for instance, Dixieland. A lot of people try to make a big point between what they call New Orleans…
Well, which came first, the colored movement towards ragtime and blues or the white movement towards ragtime and blues, or were they simultaneous?

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: Well, he does, as of the last discussion we had.

ctx.x: And I was going to ask you whether he agrees with you on your theory of jazz.
Well, he does, as of the last discussion we had.
